```{r}
d_mpi_other <- get_diag(s_mpi, lab_other)
d_mpi_mrot  <- get_diag(s_mpi, lab_mrot)

d_uni_ineff <- get_diag(s_uni, lab_ineff)
d_uni_other <- get_diag(s_uni, lab_other)
d_uni_mrot  <- get_diag(s_uni, lab_mrot)

d_wes_ineff <- get_diag(s_wes, lab_ineff)
d_wes_other <- get_diag(s_wes, lab_other)
d_wes_mrot  <- get_diag(s_wes, lab_mrot)

# off-diagonal moves
get_move <- function(tab, local_lab, global_lab) {
  stopifnot(local_lab %in% rownames(tab), global_lab %in% colnames(tab))
  n     <- tab[local_lab, global_lab]
  denom <- sum(tab[, global_lab])
  list(n = as.numeric(n), denom = as.numeric(denom), prop = as.numeric(n) / as.numeric(denom))
}

tab_mpi <- confusion_by_site[[s_mpi]]
tab_uni <- confusion_by_site[[s_uni]]
tab_wes <- confusion_by_site[[s_wes]]

# Rotation globally assigned to Other Effective locally
mpi_mrot2other <- get_move(tab_mpi, lab_other, lab_mrot)
wes_mrot2other <- get_move(tab_wes, lab_other, lab_mrot)

# Other Effective globally assigned to Rotation locally
uni_other2mrot <- get_move(tab_uni, lab_mrot, lab_other)

# pre-computed scalars for inline R
wes_pct_agree  <- fmt_pct(a_wes$pct_agree)
wes_ari        <- fmt_num(a_wes$ARI)
wes_n          <- a_wes$n
uni_pct_agree  <- fmt_pct(a_uni$pct_agree)
uni_ari        <- fmt_num(a_uni$ARI)
mpi_pct_agree  <- fmt_pct(a_mpi$pct_agree)
mpi_ari        <- fmt_num(a_mpi$ARI)

mpi_mrot_recall  <- round(d_mpi_mrot$recall, 2)
mpi_mrot_purity  <- round(d_mpi_mrot$purity, 2)
mpi_ineff_recall <- round(d_mpi_ineff$recall, 2)

uni_mrot_recall  <- round(d_uni_mrot$recall, 2)
uni_mrot_purity  <- round(d_uni_mrot$purity, 2)

wes_mrot_recall  <- round(d_wes_mrot$recall, 2)
wes_mrot_purity  <- round(d_wes_mrot$purity, 2)
wes_ineff_recall <- round(d_wes_ineff$recall, 2)
wes_flip_recall  <- round(d_wes_other$recall, 2)
```

### Cross-Cultural Consistency of Strategy Profiles
We next examined whether the continuum structure is recoverable within each site independently by re-running the k-means procedure separately within each site and computing agreement between the local and global profile assignments for each participant, using percent agreement (the proportion of participants assigned to the same profile by both solutions) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), alongside per-profile recall and purity.

Uniandes-co showed the strongest overall recovery (percent agreement = `r uni_pct_agree`, ARI = `r uni_ari`), with high recall and purity across all three profiles — including the Rotation profile (recall = `r uni_mrot_recall`, purity = `r uni_mrot_purity`). This suggests the full continuum structure is locally recoverable when sample sizes are adequate and testing conditions are consistent.

Mpieva-de showed moderate overall agreement (`r mpi_pct_agree`, ARI = `r mpi_ari`), driven primarily by poor recovery of the Ineffective profile locally (recall = `r mpi_ineff_recall`). Notably, the Rotation profile was well-recovered in mpieva-de (recall = `r mpi_mrot_recall`, purity = `r mpi_mrot_purity`), suggesting the finer subdivision within the effective end of the continuum is detectable there. The lower overall agreement at mpieva-de may reflect the greater RT variability introduced by its remote, home-based testing format.

Western-ca showed the lowest overall agreement (`r wes_pct_agree`, ARI = `r wes_ari`), but for a qualitatively different reason. The local solution assigned the large majority of children to a single group that mapped onto the global Rotation profile — producing near-perfect recall for that profile (`r wes_mrot_recall`) but low purity (`r wes_mrot_purity`), and near-zero recall for both the Ineffective (`r wes_ineff_recall`) and Matching/Flipping/Other (`r wes_flip_recall`) profiles. This pattern suggests the local solution in western-ca collapsed the full continuum into a single dominant region rather than failing to recover any particular profile. The smaller sample size at western-ca likely contributed to this instability.

# Discussion
The central aim of this study was to establish whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task measures the same underlying construct across three culturally diverse sites. The answer, across four distinct levels of analysis, is largely yes. The task achieves scalar measurement invariance — including across a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South — indicating that both the ordering and spacing of items on the latent scale are consistent across cultural contexts [@putnick2016measurement]. The angular disparity effect replicates robustly for 3D stimuli across all three sites, and is present though attenuated for 2D stimuli, providing process-level evidence that performance is driven by the spatial demands of the task in the way theory predicts [@shepard1971mental] — a form of evidence that is distinct from, and complementary to, the psychometric result. The absence of a main effect of sex or any age-by-sex interaction is consistent with the meta-analytic picture for child-friendly tasks in this age range [@lauer2019development], and its replication across all three international sites extends prior null findings beyond the Western convenience samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. And at the level of individual behavioral profiles, the broad distinction between children who disengage from the task's spatial demands and those who engage effectively is recoverable within each site independently, even if the finer subdivision between engagement types shows more variable local recovery. That these convergent forms of evidence emerge across geographically and culturally diverse samples supports the interpretation that the task is capturing individual differences in a common/universal spatial reasoning construct rather than one that is specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was developed.

## Cross-Site Invariance
Turning to our first research question, the demonstration of scalar invariance under a 2PL model establishes that the mental rotation task functions comparably across pilot sites — that items are ordered by difficulty and discrimination in the same way for children in Bogotá as for children in Leipzig or London, Ontario, and that ability estimates can be placed on a common latent scale [@putnick2016measurement]. This is a meaningful result: tasks developed in one context do not automatically achieve psychometric equivalence when administered elsewhere [@van2004bias], and the inclusion of a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South makes this a stronger test than studies conducted entirely within high-income North American and European samples. That said, scalar invariance establishes metric comparability rather than cultural equivalence in any deeper sense. With only one non-Western site — though one spanning both urban and rural schools, representing a meaningfully different cultural and socioeconomic context from the German and Canadian samples — the present findings should be treated as an encouraging foundation rather than evidence of broad cross-cultural portability. Further validation across more culturally and socioeconomically diverse sites will be needed before stronger claims can be made. The LEVANTE project is expanding to include additional sites in low- and middle-income countries in coming years, which will provide the opportunity to subject these findings to a more demanding cross-cultural test. Finally, given that LEVANTE sites differ substantially in sampling, recruitment, and testing format, site level performance differences are not interpreted here regardless of the invariance results; however, we believe the consistency of patterns within and across sites remains informative.

## Angular Sensitivity
Our second research question asked whether performance is driven by the spatial properties of the stimuli. The key benchmark here is the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental: as the rotational distance between a 3D target and its match increases, so too does the time required to judge whether they correspond. This relationship, among the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology [@cooper1973chronometric; @peters2008applications], has been demonstrated extensively in children and adults from middle-to-high-income Western convenience samples [@kaltner2016developmental; @jansen2015role], but had not previously been established in culturally diverse samples of children. Its consistent emergence here, across all three sites, suggests that the underlying cognitive process it indexes — the spatially continuous transformation of object orientation — is not specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was originally documented. This matters because psychometric equivalence and process-level validity are distinct forms of evidence. It is one thing to show that a task achieves comparable difficulty ordering across sites; it is another to show that performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of the stimuli in the way that mental rotation theory predicts [@borsboom2004concept]. The angular disparity effect provides the latter, and its cross-cultural replication substantially strengthens the case that the task is engaging spatial cognition specifically, rather than some culturally-variable combination of task-general skills. The shallower slope for 2D stimuli likely reflects the greater familiarity of duck and rabbit silhouettes relative to the 3D geometric shapes: when stimuli are easy to tell apart, children can make same/different judgments by comparing surface features rather than rotating, producing a weaker RT–angle relationship [@folk1987effects; @bethell1988mental].

Children at mpieva-de showed both higher baseline response times and steeper absolute RT–angle slopes than the other two sites — a pattern consistent with a testing format explanation rather than a genuine cultural difference in angular sensitivity. Remote home-based testing on family devices, as used at mpieva-de, may introduce environmental variability that is likely to inflate both baseline RT and trial-to-trial noise; because absolute slopes scale with baseline speed, this would mechanically produce steeper slopes even without greater rotation sensitivity, a pattern visible in the wider raw RT distributions at mpieva-de (see [Appendix C (Raw RT by age and site)](#sec-apx-irt-ability-age)).

## Sex Differences
Our third research question asked whether sex differences in mental rotation ability are detectable in this sample, and whether any such differences interact with age. The absence of a main effect of sex or an age-by-sex interaction replicates the pattern reported in several recent studies of primary school-aged children using child-friendly mental rotation tasks [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and is consistent with the meta-analytic picture: reliable sex differences in mental rotation are small and inconsistent in this age range, particularly for tasks using 2D stimuli and child-friendly formats of the kind used here [@lauer2019development]. The LEVANTE task's design — 2D animal silhouettes alongside 3D block figures — places it squarely in the category of tasks where the meta-analytic expectation for a gender difference is modest at best. Notably, the null finding held across all three international study sites, extending prior null results beyond the middle-to-high-income Western samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. Taken together, the sex difference results are consistent with the broader argument of this paper: that the task captures a spatially-driven construct that is consistent across cultural contexts.

## Strategy Variation

Our final research question asked whether meaningful variation in how children engage with the spatial demands of the task can be identified from trial-level behavioral signatures. Research with adults has established that solvers draw on a range of strategies when performing mental rotation tasks, spanning a holistic-analytic continuum [@gluck2003spatial], and that strategy selection varies across individuals and shifts with task demands [@nazareth2019strategy]. Crucially, such strategies can be identified from behavioral signatures in RT data even in the absence of direct observation [@geiser2006separating], providing the methodological basis for the present analysis.

The clustering exercise identified three differentiable regions of this continuum, partly because the data resist clean separation and partly because, as discussed below, the continuum structure proves difficult to recover consistently within individual sites. At one end, a subset of children — labeled 'Ineffective' — show clear disengagement from the spatial structure of the task: the lowest absolute RT–angle slope of the three profiles, high response instability, and near-chance accuracy at high angular disparities. Although this group's relative slope appears elevated relative to the two effective profiles, this reflects their faster baseline processing speed inflating the ratio rather than genuine angular sensitivity — their absolute slope is the lowest of the three profiles, confirming the absence of rotation cost rather than its presence. 

The two effective profiles — Matching/Flipping/Other and Rotation — are distinguished primarily by the shape of their RT–angle functions, but not by accuracy, which was higher for the Matching/Flipping/Other group. Importantly, the two profile-defining dimensions do different separating work: ability distinguishes the Ineffective group from both effective profiles, while relative RT slope distinguishes the two effective profiles from each other — and it is this complementary structure that justifies retaining three profiles rather than two. An interesting finding is that the Rotation profile is both the most common globally (n = `r mrot_n`, `r mrot_pct`%) and yet associated with lower mean ability than the Matching/Flipping/Other group — the reverse of what the broader literature might lead us to expect [@khooshabeh2013individual; @heil2008sex], though the effect is modest and the groups overlap considerably in ability. This could suggest that RT signatures consistent with full analog rotation carry a greater cognitive cost than feature-based engagement [@just1985cognitive; @khooshabeh2013individual], particularly for the 2D stimuli where rotational demands are lower. The overlap between these two profiles in the behavioral feature space — consistent across all three dimensionality reduction methods [Appendix D (Dimensionality reduction)](#sec-apx-dimreduc) — reinforces this picture: the distinction between them is gradient rather than categorical. 

The recoverability of this continuum structure varies across sites in qualitatively different ways: uniandes-co recovered all three regions well, mpieva-de recovered the effective subdivision but showed poor recovery of the Ineffective profile — possibly reflecting the greater RT variability introduced by its remote, home-based testing format — and western-ca collapsed the full continuum into a single dominant region, likely reflecting its smaller sample size (n = `r wes_n`)` rather than a genuine absence of strategy variation. We retain the three-profile distinction in the global solution because collapsing to k = 2 obscures a theoretically meaningful difference in RT–angle profile shape, but treat it as a convenient descriptive marker rather than evidence for discrete strategy types. Taken together, the exploratory clustering exercise reveals a meaningful continuum of engagement — from children who appear to disengage from the task's spatial elements entirely, to those who solve it effectively through different spatial processes — but larger, more methodologically consistent samples will be needed before firm conclusions about cross-cultural variation in strategy profiles can be drawn.

Read alongside the measurement invariance result, these findings raise an apparent paradox — but it is resolvable. Scalar invariance establishes that between-person differences in ability are organised comparably across sites; the clustering analysis establishes that within-person processing varies. These are compatible: children can arrive at commensurable ability estimates via different cognitive routes. The invariance result does not imply a single shared cognitive process — only that whatever processes children bring to the task, the resulting ability differences are structured the same way across cultural contexts.

## Limitations
Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. Although the three sites span different continents and linguistic contexts, two of the three are middle-to-high-income Western samples, and while the Colombian site is more socioeconomically diverse — spanning urban schools in Bogotá and rural schools in surrounding departments — the sample as a whole remains far from representative of the full range of cultural environments in which children develop. The LEVANTE project has already expanded to six additional sites since this initial data collection, with future efforts prioritizing data collection in low- and middle-income countries, which will substantially broaden the cultural scope of findings like those reported here. Sample sizes were also unbalanced across sites, with the Canadian sample smaller overall, which limits the precision of site-level estimates and the power to detect cross-site differences. The cross-sectional design is a further constraint: developmental trajectories here are inferred from age differences between children rather than observed directly. Longitudinal data are currently being collected and processed, however, and will allow this question to be addressed more directly in due course. Finally, the strategy clustering analysis is exploratory and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The profiles are inferred from behavioral proxies rather than directly observed strategies, and replication in larger, more diverse, and more methodologically consistent samples will be needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

# Conclusion
Four research questions motivated this study, each asking in a different way whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task is doing consistent and interpretable work across culturally diverse settings. Across all four, the answer is largely affirmative. Scalar measurement invariance holds across sites including a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South; the angular disparity effect replicates as a process-level signature of spatial engagement; sex differences are absent in a pattern consistent with the meta-analytic picture for this age range and task type; and a meaningful continuum of engagement strategies is detectable, at least in broad outline, across all three sites. These findings do not mean that mental rotation development is uniform across children or contexts — the substantial individual variability within sites, and the tentative evidence for cross-cultural differences in strategy distributions, suggest there is much still to understand about what drives variation in spatial ability across children. But they do mean that the task is measuring something consistent — that when a child in Bogotá, a child in Leipzig, and a child in London (Ontario) sit down to judge whether two rotated objects are the same, they are, by and large, making use of the same general set of spatial abilities. Such consistency is the foundation on which meaningful cross-cultural comparisons can be built.

## Within-person dynamics {#sec-apx-within-person-dynamics}
Having established that 3D stimuli elicit a clear angular disparity effect while 2D stimuli do to a lesser extent, we next asked a complementary question: whether children show sensitivity to task demands as they unfold in real time — specifically, whether reaction times shift systematically at the transition from 2D to 3D stimuli, and whether practice effects are detectable within blocks. To isolate time-on-task effects from item-driven RT changes, we residualized log-RTs on angle, stimulus, and item type prior to analysis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-within-person-trials
#| fig-cap: "**Trial-level reaction time dynamics (angle-residualised).** Mean residual log-RT across trials for each non-adaptive site ±SE. The dashed line marks the 2D→3D transition. Retest and CAT data removed."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# # prep: remove CAT data
# trial_resid_data <- mrot_rt_trial |>
#   filter(!adaptive, correct == 1)
# 
# # residualize log_rt on angle + stimulus + item_group
# resid_model <- lm(log_rt ~ angle + stimulus + item_group, 
#                   data = trial_resid_data)
# 
# trial_resid_data <- trial_resid_data |>
#   mutate(log_rt_resid = residuals(resid_model),
#          block = item_group |> str_to_upper())

trial_resid_data <- mrot_lme_data |>
  mutate(log_rt_resid = residuals(full_mod),
         block = item_group |> str_to_upper())

trial_resid_data |>
  group_by(run_id, item_group) |>
  summarise(start = min(trial_number), end = max(trial_number)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # filter(item_group == "3d") |>
  count(item_group, start)

transition_trial <- trial_resid_data |>
  filter(item_group == "3d") |>
  pull(trial_number) |>
  min()

# plot
ggplot(trial_resid_data, 
       aes(x = trial_number, y = log_rt_resid, 
           color = site_label, fill = site_label)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = interaction(site_label, block)),
              method = "loess", span = 0.75, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = transition_trial - 0.5, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "lightgrey", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = transition_trial + 1, y = Inf,
           label = "Start of 3D block", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_pal) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = site_pal) +
  labs(
    x     = "Trial number",
    y     = "Residual reaction time",
    color = "Site",
    fill  = "Site"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: within-person-models
#| include: false

# center trial number within each block so the intercept at transition is interpretable
within_person_data <- trial_resid_data |>
  mutate(
    block         = factor(block, levels = c("2D", "3D")),
    # trial number centered within block
    trial_c       = trial_number - transition_trial,
    site_label          = factor(site_label)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(trial_number), !is.na(log_rt_resid))

# Model 1: continuous trial slope only 
m_wp_continuous <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 2: add block as main effect — tests for discontinuous jump at transition
m_wp_jump <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 3: add trial × block interaction — tests whether slope changes after transition
m_wp_slope <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c * block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# model comparisons
anova_wp_jump  <- anova(m_wp_continuous, m_wp_jump)   # is there a jump?
anova_wp_slope <- anova(m_wp_jump, m_wp_slope)  

# extract key numbers
wp_coefs       <- coef(summary(m_wp_slope))

# block jump (intercept shift at transition)
beta_wp_block  <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_block    <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_block     <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# within-block trial slope (2D block)
beta_wp_trial  <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Estimate"]
se_wp_trial    <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_trial     <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# interaction: does slope differ in 3D block?
beta_wp_int    <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_int      <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_int       <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# anova numbers for inline reporting
wp_jump_chisq  <- anova_wp_jump$Chisq[2]
wp_jump_df     <- anova_wp_jump$Df[2]
wp_jump_p      <- anova_wp_jump[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]

wp_slope_chisq <- anova_wp_slope$Chisq[2]
wp_slope_df    <- anova_wp_slope$Df[2]
wp_slope_p     <- anova_wp_slope[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]
```


@fig-within-person-trials plots mean residual log-RT across trials for each site. To test for a discontinuous shift in RT at the 2D→3D block transition and for within-block practice effects, we fitted a series of mixed-effects models predicting residual log-RT from trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes.

First, a model including a block indicator (2D vs 3D) significantly improved fit over a continuous trial-slope model (χ²(`r wp_jump_df`) = `r round(wp_jump_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_jump_p)`), confirming that the increase in RT at the 2D→3D transition is discontinuous rather than a continuation of a gradual trend. The block coefficient indicates a sudden upward shift in residual RT at trial 48 (β = `r round(beta_wp_block, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_block, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_block)`), consistent with children recalibrating their processing demands at the block boundary rather than adapting incrementally.

Second, within each block, RTs decreased across trials, indicating a practice effect operating independently of angular disparity (β = `r round(beta_wp_trial, 4)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_trial, 4)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_trial)`). Adding a trial × block interaction `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, "significantly improved model fit", "did not significantly improve model fit")` (χ²(`r wp_slope_df`) = `r round(wp_slope_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_slope_p)`) `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, paste0(", with the within-block acceleration differing between the 2D and 3D blocks (β = ", round(beta_wp_int, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_wp_int, 3), ", p ", fmt_p(p_wp_int), ")"), "")`. Both patterns — the discontinuous block transition and the within-block acceleration — were qualitatively consistent across all three sites, further extending the cross-cultural consistency observed in the angular disparity analysis.

The Ineffective profile is characterized by near-zero slope and high response instability rather than slow or fast processing per se. ## Cluster solution validation {#sec-apx-cluster}
To assess the appropriateness of the three-profile solution, we evaluated cluster quality across k = 1–8 using two complementary metrics: total within-cluster sum of squares (the elbow method) and average silhouette width (@fig-k-sweep-validation). The silhouette analysis identified k = 2 as the statistically optimal solution, with average silhouette width peaking at 0.35 before declining steeply at k = 3 and remaining low thereafter. The elbow plot showed a moderate inflection at k = 3, after which additional clusters yielded diminishing reductions in within-cluster variance. To examine whether k = 2 was substantively adequate, we examined the RT–angle functions of the resulting two-cluster solution (@fig-k2-cluster-check). The higher-ability cluster displayed a characteristic inverted-U RT function, rising to a peak around 120° before declining at 160° — a pattern that, in the three-cluster solution, distinguishes the Matching/Flipping/Other and Rotation groups. This indicates that k = 2 collapses two distinguishable effective engagement profiles into a single region, obscuring a theoretically meaningful behavioral difference. We therefore adopted k = 3 on both empirical grounds (the elbow inflection) and theoretical grounds (the interpretability of the resulting RT profiles), noting that the three profiles are treated as convenient descriptive anchors along a continuum rather than evidence for discrete strategy types.

```{r}
#| label: fig-k-sweep-validation
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "**Cluster validation metrics: Elbow Method (left) and Silhouette Analysis (right).** The elbow plot shows a bend at k = 3, and silhouette width peaks at k = 2 before declining, providing partial support for the 3-cluster solution."

.theme <- theme_get()
p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8, linecolor = pal$grey) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, color = pal$grey) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Total within sum of squares") +
  .theme

p_sil <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8, linecolor = pal$grey) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Average silhouette width") +
  .theme

grid.arrange(p_elbow, p_sil, nrow = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-k2-cluster-check
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**RT–angle functions for the k = 2 solution.** The higher-ability cluster displays an inverted-U RT curve consistent with a mix of Rotation and Matching/Flipping/Other engagement profiles, suggesting that k = 2 collapses two distinguishable effective profiles into a single region."

# Set up Input (same features as main analysis)
analysis_data_k2 <- rich_features_final |>
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Baseline_Speed, Abs_Slope, Rel_Slope, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

global_input_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 |>
  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Instability, Abs_Slope, Learning_Rate) |>
  scale()

# Run K-Means with k = 2 
set.seed(123)
k_global_2 <- kmeans(global_input_k2, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
analysis_data_k2$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global_2$cluster)

# Label the 2 Clusters 
# We define them simply by Ability (Low vs High) since we can't split by slope yet
cluster_stats_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 |>
  group_by(Global_Cluster) |>
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Identify Lower Ability Cluster
low_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 |> arrange(mean_ability) |> slice(1) |> pull(Global_Cluster)
# The other one is High Efficiency
high_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 |> arrange(desc(mean_ability)) |> slice(1) |> pull(Global_Cluster)

analysis_data_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 |>
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    Global_Cluster == low_eff_id ~ "Low Efficacy (Cluster 2)",
    Global_Cluster == high_eff_id ~ "High Efficacy (Cluster 1)"
  ))

k2_colors <- c(
  "Low Efficacy (Cluster 2)"  = strategy_pal[1],
  "High Efficacy (Cluster 1)" = strategy_pal[3]
)

# Plot the Curves (Visual Check)
# Join labels to raw data
rt_by_strategy_k2 <- mrot_rich_data |>
  left_join(
    analysis_data_k2 |> select(run_id, Strategy_Label),
    by = c("run_id")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Label), is.finite(log_rt), is.finite(angle))

# Calculate User Means
rt_user_angle_k2 <- rt_by_strategy_k2 |>
  group_by(Strategy_Label, run_id, angle) |>
  summarise(user_mean_log_rt = mean(log_rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Calculate Group Means
rt_summary_k2 <- rt_user_angle_k2 |>
  group_by(Strategy_Label, angle) |>
  summarise(
    n_users     = n_distinct(run_id),
    mean_log_rt = mean(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_log_rt   = sd(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_users),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot
ggplot(rt_summary_k2, aes(x = angle, y = mean_log_rt, colour = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_log_rt - 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  ymax = mean_log_rt + 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  fill = Strategy_Label), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  labs(
    title    = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    y = "Mean log reaction time (s)",
    # y = "Mean log(RT) (participant-weighted)", 
    x = "Rotation angle (°)",
    colour = "Strategy", fill = "Strategy"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Strategy use across age groups {#sec-apx-strategy-age-group}
```{r}
#| label: strategy-age-data
#| include: false

strategy_by_age <- analysis_data |>
  count(age_group, Strategy_Label) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 2)) |>
  ungroup()

get_prop <- function(age_grp, strategy) {
  strategy_by_age[
    strategy_by_age$age_group == age_grp & 
    strategy_by_age$Strategy_Label == strategy, 
    "prop"
  ][[1]]
}

# pre-computed scalars for inline R
ineff_pct_young <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Ineffective") * 100
ineff_pct_mid   <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Ineffective") * 100
ineff_pct_old   <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Ineffective") * 100
flip_pct_young  <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Matching/Flipping/Other") * 100
flip_pct_mid    <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Matching/Flipping/Other") * 100
flip_pct_old    <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Matching/Flipping/Other") * 100
mrot_pct_young  <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Rotation") * 100
mrot_pct_mid    <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Rotation") * 100
mrot_pct_old    <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Rotation") * 100
```
We examined whether the distribution of engagement profiles varied across age groups (@fig-strategy-by-age). This analysis is purely descriptive — formal inferential testing would be circular given that both the age groupings and profile assignments are derived from the data, and the profile solution itself carries the caveats described above. With those caveats in mind, a descriptive pattern is nonetheless visible. The proportion of children assigned to the Ineffective profile declined substantially with age, from `r ineff_pct_young`% in the youngest group (ages 5–8.3) to `r ineff_pct_mid`% (ages 8.3–10.6) and `r ineff_pct_old`% (ages 10.6–13.7). This was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the Matching/Flipping/Other profile, from `r flip_pct_young`% to `r flip_pct_mid`% and `r flip_pct_old`%. By contrast, the proportion assigned to the Rotation profile remained consistent across age groups (`r mrot_pct_young`%, `r mrot_pct_mid`%, `r mrot_pct_old`%). The primary developmental shift thus appears to be a move away from task disengagement toward effective feature-matching engagement profiles, with the proportion showing analog rotation signatures remaining comparatively stable across this age range.

```{r}
strategy_by_age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = prop, fill = fct_rev(Strategy_Label))) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
                    # labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Age group (years)",
       y = "Proportion in strategy profile",
       fill = "Strategy") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.direction = "vertical")
```

## Dimensionality reduction checks {#sec-apx-dimreduc}
To validate the continuum structure, we examined whether the three-profile solution was recoverable using alternative dimensionality reduction methods: PCA (@fig-pca-check), t-SNE (@fig-tsne-check), and UMAP (@fig-umap-check). PCA loadings were also inspected to characterize the underlying feature structure (@fig-pca-loadings).

Results were consistent across all three methods in one key respect: the Ineffective group was clearly and reliably separated from the two effective engagement profiles, appearing as a distinct region in all three projections — the right end of PC1 in the PCA, and distinct regions in the t-SNE and UMAP projections. This convergent separation provides strong evidence that this group occupies a genuinely distinct region of the feature space. The boundary between the Rotation and Matching/Flipping/Other profiles was, however, substantially less clear. Green and blue points overlapped considerably across all three visualizations, suggesting these two profiles represent adjacent regions of a continuum rather than fully discrete groupings — a finding consistent with the silhouette analysis favoring k = 2.

Inspection of the PCA loadings offered interpretive support for the feature set. PC1 loaded positively on Instability and Relative Slope, and negatively on Baseline Speed, Absolute Slope, and Learning Rate, reflecting a dimension that contrasts inefficient, variable engagement (high instability, elevated relative slope, slow baseline) with efficient, consistent processing (fast baseline, steeper absolute slope, stronger learning across trials). This dimension primarily separates the Ineffective group from the two effective profiles. PC2 loaded most strongly on Relative Slope and Absolute Slope — both positive — with Learning Rate loading negatively, reflecting a rotation cost dimension that captures angular sensitivity largely independent of general processing speed. This dimension provides the primary separation between the two effective profiles. The fact that these two components map onto theoretically meaningful and distinct dimensions provides confidence that the clustering features are not redundant.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tsne-check
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "**t-SNE visualization of engagement profiles.** The Ineffective group forms a distinct region, while the Rotation and Matching/Flipping/Other profiles show considerable overlap, suggesting softer boundaries between the two effective engagement profiles."

tsne_input <- analysis_data |>
    select(run_id, Learning_Rate, Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Instability) |>
    distinct() |> 
    na.omit()

set.seed(42) 
tsne_result <- Rtsne(
    as.matrix(tsne_input |> select(-run_id)), 
    dims = 2, perplexity = 30, verbose = FALSE, max_iter = 500
)

tsne_plot_data <- tsne_input |>
    mutate(tSNE_1 = tsne_result$Y[,1], tSNE_2 = tsne_result$Y[,2]) |>
    left_join(analysis_data |> select(run_id, Strategy_Label), by = "run_id")

ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = tSNE_1, y = tSNE_2, color = Strategy_Label)) +
  # coord_fixed() +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors,
                       labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 25)) +
    labs(title = NULL, x = "Dimension 1", y = "Dimension 2", color = "Strategy") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-check
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "**PCA projection of the five clustering features colored by engagement profile.** The Ineffective group separates clearly along PC1, while the Rotation and Matching/Flipping/Other profiles overlap along both components."

pca_result <- prcomp(tsne_input |> select(-run_id), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pca_plot_data <- tsne_input |>
    mutate(PC1 = pca_result$x[,1], PC2 = pca_result$x[,2]) |>
    left_join(analysis_data |> select(run_id, Strategy_Label), by = "run_id")

ggplot(pca_plot_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Strategy_Label)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1) +

    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Full 0–360° angle check {#sec-apx-e}

The primary analyses modeled angular disparity as the shortest path to upright, capped at 180°, on the assumption that participants take the most efficient route when rotating stimuli. To test this assumption, we re-ran the clustering using full 0–360° rotation angles and plotted RT and accuracy functions across the complete angular range (@fig-rt-angle-by-strategy-360, @fig-accuracy-angle-by-strategy-360). We verified that the angular disparity variable was correctly computed, confirming that full rotation angles were accurately recoded to their shortest-path equivalents (e.g., a 320° rotation has a disparity of 40°). The 360° clustering produced identical profile assignments to the main analysis (Ineffective: n = 228; Rotation: n = 511; Matching/Flipping/Other: n = 419), confirming that the robustness check is examining the same profiles under a different angle representation.

The results were broadly consistent with the disparity-based analyses and provided direct support for the shortest-path assumption. Both the Rotation and Matching/Flipping/Other profiles showed RT functions that increased from 40° to a peak around 200–240°, then declined as angles approached 320°, forming the expected near-symmetric inverted-U around 180°. This pattern is what would be predicted if participants always rotate via the shorter available path, and would not be expected under a fixed-direction rotation strategy.

The Rotation profile showed the steeper and higher RT function throughout, rising from a mean log RT of 1.02 at 40° to a peak of 1.85 at 240° before declining to 1.49 at 320°. The Matching/Flipping/Other profile rose more gradually, peaking at 1.46 at 240° — consistent with less angular sensitivity relative to baseline speed, as reflected in its shallower relative slope in the main analysis. Notably, the inverted-U shape of the Matching/Flipping/Other profile in the full 360° data is more symmetric than the 120° peak-and-decline pattern observed in the disparity-capped data, suggesting the apparent flipping signature in the main analysis may partly reflect the capping of angles at 180° rather than a pure reflective symmetry strategy. Accuracy for both effective profiles showed a corresponding U-shaped function, declining to a minimum around 160–200° before recovering at higher angles, with the Matching/Flipping/Other profile maintaining the highest accuracy throughout. The Ineffective profile again showed a broadly flat and declining RT function across the full angular range, with accuracy remaining low at peak angles and showing only a modest recovery above 240°, further supporting the interpretation that these children are not engaging with the spatial structure of the items.
```{r}
#| label: robustness-check-all-angles
#| results: "hide"

# NOTE: all objects in this and subsequent 360° chunks use _360 suffixes to avoid overwriting main analysis objects. These chunks must remain the
# last substantive analysis chunks in the document.

mrot_rich_data_360 <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  rename(ang_disparity = angle,
         angle = angle_full) |>
  mutate(
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(ang_disparity)),
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

contrasts(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus))

m_rich_360 <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_s * stimulus + trial_s +
    (1 + angle_s + trial_s | run_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mrot_rich_data_360,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 20000))
)

ran_effs_360 <- ranef(m_rich_360)$run_id |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("run_id") |>
  rename(
    int_dev   = `(Intercept)`,
    slope_dev = angle_s,
    trial_dev = trial_s
  )

fix_int_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["(Intercept)"]
fix_ang_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["angle_s"]
fix_tri_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["trial_s"]

rich_features_raw_360 <- ran_effs_360 |>
  mutate(
    Baseline_Speed = fix_int_360 + int_dev,
    Abs_Slope      = fix_ang_360 + slope_dev,
    Rel_Slope      = Abs_Slope / Baseline_Speed,
    Learning_Rate  = fix_tri_360 + trial_dev
  )

mrot_rich_data_360$resid <- residuals(m_rich_360)

instability_data_360 <- mrot_rich_data_360 |>
  group_by(run_id) |>
  summarise(
    Instability = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rich_features_final_360 <- rich_features_raw_360 |>
  left_join(instability_data_360, by = "run_id") |>
  left_join(ability_run, by = "run_id") |>
  mutate(Site = site_label) |>
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Baseline_Speed, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

# Check: ang_disparity should never exceed 180
summary(mrot_rich_data_360$ang_disparity)

# Spot check a few items
mrot_rich_data_360 |>
  select(item, item_original, angle, ang_disparity) |>
  distinct() |>
  arrange(item_original) |>
  head(20)
  
```

```{r}
#| label: clustering-execution-360
#| include: false

# strategy_colors <- c(
#   "Ineffective" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[1],
#   "Matching/Flipping/Other" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[2], 
#   "Rotation" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[3]  
# )

analysis_data_360 <- rich_features_final_360 |>
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, 
                  Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

global_input_360 <- analysis_data_360 |>
  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, 
         Instability, Learning_Rate) |>
  scale()

set.seed(123)
k_global_360 <- kmeans(global_input_360, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
analysis_data_360$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global_360$cluster)

cluster_stats_360 <- analysis_data_360 |>
  group_by(Global_Cluster) |>
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability),
    mean_slope   = mean(Rel_Slope), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

low_eff_id_360 <- cluster_stats_360 |>
  arrange(mean_ability) |> slice(1) |> pull(Global_Cluster)

effective_clusters_360 <- cluster_stats_360 |>
  filter(Global_Cluster != low_eff_id_360) |>
  arrange(mean_slope)

analytical_id_360 <- effective_clusters_360 |> slice(1) |> pull(Global_Cluster)
holistic_id_360   <- effective_clusters_360 |> slice(2) |> pull(Global_Cluster)

analysis_data_360 <- analysis_data_360 |>
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    Global_Cluster == low_eff_id_360    ~ "Ineffective",
    Global_Cluster == analytical_id_360 ~ "Matching/Flipping/Other",
    Global_Cluster == holistic_id_360   ~ "Rotation"
  ))

ggplot(analysis_data_360, aes(x = ability, y = Rel_Slope, color = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Cluster Result: Ability vs. Relative Slope (full 0-360° angles)",
    x = "Ability", y = "Relative Slope"
  )
```

```{r}
  left_join(
    analysis_data_360 |> select(run_id, Strategy_Label),
    by = "run_id"

rt_user_angle_360 <- rt_by_strategy_360 |>

rt_angle_person_summary_360 <- rt_user_angle_360 |>

    .groups = "drop"

missing_cols <- setdiff(levels(rt_angle_person_summary_360$Strategy_Label), names(strategy_colors))
stopifnot(length(missing_cols) == 0)

  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +

    aes(ymin = mean_log_rt - 1.96 * se_log_rt,
        ymax = mean_log_rt + 1.96 * se_log_rt,
        fill = Strategy_Label),
    alpha = 0.15, colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n_users), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = strategy_colors, drop = FALSE,
    labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 25)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = strategy_colors, drop = FALSE,
    labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 25)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160, 200, 240, 280, 320, 360)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    x = "Rotation angle (°)",
    y = "Mean log reaction time (s)",
    colour = "Strategy", fill = "Strategy"
  )
```

\clearpage
Mental rotation — the ability to mentally transform an object's orientation in space — is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive psychology, yet evidence for its cross-cultural validity in children remains limited. We examined performance on the LEVANTE (Learning Variability Network Exchange) mental rotation task across three international study sites (Colombia, Germany, and Canada) in `{r} n_final$n_users` children aged 5--13 years (`{r} overall_sex_counts$Female` girls, `{r} overall_sex_counts$Male` boys, `{r} overall_sex_counts$Unknown` unknown). The task demonstrated measurement invariance across all three sites (2PL scalar invariance model; ΔBIC = `{r} delta_bic_configural` vs. configural invariance model). The angular disparity effect (@shepard1971mental) replicated robustly for 3D stimuli (), with a 90° increase in rotation angle associated with approximately 45% longer response times; the effect was present but attenuated for 2D stimuli (). No main effect of sex was detected (). Exploratory clustering identified three engagement profiles: Rotation (monotonically increasing RT–angle function), Matching/Flipping/Other, and Ineffective (absent angular sensitivity, low ability). These findings establish that the task captures a consistent, spatially-driven construct across culturally diverse samples — a necessary precondition for using cross-cultural data to understand variation in spatial reasoning.
